title: Blind hearts
hook: it is not the eyes that go blind but the hearts in the chests (22:46)

segments.voice: Yesterday, neither flesh nor blood, and your line was only the heart reaches him. What did you find when you checked the reason behind a gift? Day four hundred eighty-seven.

A caravan route in Arabia runs past ruins. A well with nobody drawing from it. A tall, strong building with no one living inside. Travelers pass them on the way north to Syria, water the camels nearby, maybe glance up. They've seen them a hundred times. They're scenery. Surah Al-Hajj points at exactly this kind of place: a town that's fallen in on its own roofs, a deserted well, a lofty tower. And then it asks the travelers a question about their own eyes.

Verse forty-six begins with a question: haven't they traveled in the land, so that they might have hearts to understand with, and ears to hear with? Then the line this day is named for. Pickthall: "For indeed it is not the eyes that grow blind, but it is the hearts, which are within the bosoms, that grow blind." Their eyes work perfectly. They saw the ruins. What didn't happen is understanding. The verse puts seeing somewhere other than the eyes. In the Qur'an, the heart, qalb, isn't mainly the seat of feelings, the way it often is in English. It's where a person understands, decides, takes things in. The word comes from a root about turning over, and hearts in this picture are the part of you that can turn. A hadith in Bukhari says there is a piece of flesh in the body: if it's sound, the whole body is sound, and if it's corrupt, the whole body is corrupt, and that piece is the heart. Notice the odd little phrase, the hearts within the bosoms, the hearts in the chests. Everyone knows where hearts are. Commentators suggest the extra words are there for force: this is the real heart we mean, the one inside you, not a figure of speech. So the verse isn't scolding anyone for poor eyesight. It's describing the most ordinary kind of blindness, the kind that comes from familiarity. The ruin you pass daily. The person you've stopped really looking at. The sky you haven't checked in weeks.
screen: `TRAVELERS WHO SAW THE RUINS.` · `NOT THE EYES THAT GO BLIND.` · `THE QALB: WHERE YOU UNDERSTAND.` · `BLINDNESS BY FAMILIARITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at something with fresh eyes. Sit, and let the breath settle. Pick one thing in front of you that you see every day. A mug, your hand, the view from the window. Look at it as if you'd just arrived from very far away. Where did it come from? Who made it? What has it been through? Let your eyes rest there, and let the understanding catch up. If you pray, you can ask for a seeing heart. The bell holds the time.
Blind hearts. In Surah Al-Hajj, it isn't the eyes that go blind, but the hearts within the chests: seeing without understanding. Today's word.
Your line: hearts see. Today, on a route you take all the time, notice one thing you've walked past a hundred times, and ask what it's telling you. Day four hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Muslim teachers often quote 22:46 when speaking about reflection, and the Qur'an's repeated call to travel and consider the ruins of past peoples is part of how many Muslims think about history.

fork.setup: you've passed the same ruined town on every caravan trip for years. what does the surah want you to do with it?
options: avoid that route; ruins are bad luck.
stop seeing scenery, and let it make you understand.

fork.reveal: travel so that you have hearts to understand with. the eyes had already seen it; the heart hadn't.

original.note: Arabic: the hearts; singular qalb, from a root about turning over.

trapdoor: what you thought: blind hearts means cold, unfeeling people.
what it means: people who see with their eyes but don't understand, because the heart is where understanding happens.
what a scholar hears: qalb (root q-l-b, to turn); 'allati fi s-sudur' (within the chests) read by commentators as emphasis; compare the hadith of the mudgha, the piece of flesh, in Bukhari 52.
